category: The -en plurals and the odd ones left over

entries.meaning: A young human, or anyone's son or daughter at any age.
examples: The child fell asleep in the car.
Six children were playing in the yard.
She has been teaching young children for twenty years.
Both of their children live overseas now.
He is the only child of a famous architect.
She's a child of the nineties and it shows.
The whole design is a child of its era.

senses.head: A young human being
examples: The child fell asleep in the car.
Six children were playing in the yard.
She has been teaching young children for twenty years.

senses.head: A son or daughter, regardless of age
body: Here child says nothing about age — a sixty-year-old is still someone's child. (сын или дочь)
examples: Both of their children live overseas now.
He is the only child of a famous architect.

senses.head: Someone shaped by a particular time or place
body: Figurative, usually followed by of. (дитя, порождение)
examples: She's a child of the nineties and it shows.
The whole design is a child of its era.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the children are asleep
entries.contrast: The vowel shortens in the plural: singular /aɪ/ as in mild, plural /ɪ/ as in chill. Saying ✗ /ˈtʃaɪldrən/ is the commonest learner error. ✗ childs and ✗ childrens are both wrong — the possessive is children's.

entries.meaning: A domesticated bull used for pulling loads; more broadly, cattle of the genus Bos.
examples: A single ox can pull an astonishing weight.
Two oxen dragged the cart out of the mud.
The museum has a wagon with a full oxen team.
He's as strong as an ox.
The oxen were yoked in pairs before dawn.

senses.head: The draft animal
examples: A single ox can pull an astonishing weight.
Two oxen dragged the cart out of the mud.
The museum has a wagon with a full oxen team.

senses.head: In compounds and comparisons
examples: He's as strong as an ox.
The oxen were yoked in pairs before dawn.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the oxen were yoked together
entries.contrast: ✗ oxes is wrong. This is the last fully regular -en plural in the language. Note that box → boxes and fox → foxes are perfectly regular — only ox takes -en.

entries.meaning: A male sibling; by extension, a fellow member of a group.
examples: My brother teaches high school chemistry.
She has three brothers and no sisters.
The two brothers opened a restaurant together.
The brethren gathered for the evening service.
He addressed his union brothers and sisters.
Thanks, brother — I owe you one.
Oh brother, here we go again.

senses.head: A male sibling
examples: My brother teaches high school chemistry.
She has three brothers and no sisters.
The two brothers opened a restaurant together.

senses.head: A fellow member of a community
body: Of a church, union, or fraternity. This is the sense that keeps the old plural brethren. (собрат)
examples: The brethren gathered for the evening service.
He addressed his union brothers and sisters.

senses.head: As a form of address, and as an exclamation
body: Informal American speech. (брат, братан; ну и ну)
examples: Thanks, brother — I owe you one.
Oh brother, here we go again.

entries.plural: brothers /ˈbrʌðərz/ · also brethren /ˈbrɛðrɪn/ in religious use
entries.agreement: plural verb — my brothers live nearby
entries.pattern: regular -s, with an archaic -en plural surviving in one sense
entries.variants: brothers (family) · brethren (a religious or fraternal body)
entries.contrast: The two plurals are not interchangeable. Family members are always brothers. Brethren refers to fellow members of a church, order, or society, and using it of your siblings sounds like a joke.

entries.meaning: A human being. The word every learner needs and the plural nobody guesses.
examples: One person was waiting at the counter.
Twelve people signed up for the class.
She's the kindest person I know.
The elevator holds eight persons.
Police are looking for two persons of interest.
The Sámi are an indigenous people of northern Europe.
The exhibit covers the peoples of the Pacific Northwest.
Spanish marks person on every verb ending.

senses.head: A human being
examples: One person was waiting at the counter.
Twelve people signed up for the class.
She's the kindest person I know.

senses.head: persons — the official plural
body: Legal documents, notices, and law enforcement. In ordinary speech it sounds stiff or bureaucratic. (лица)
examples: The elevator holds eight persons.
Police are looking for two persons of interest.

senses.head: people — a nation or ethnic group
body: A separate countable noun with a regular plural. (народ)
examples: The Sámi are an indigenous people of northern Europe.
The exhibit covers the peoples of the Pacific Northwest.

senses.head: In grammar — first, second, third person
examples: Spanish marks person on every verb ending.

entries.plural: people /ˈpiːpəl/ · also persons /ˈpɜːrsənz/ in legal and official use
entries.pattern: suppletive — the plural is a different word
entries.contrast: People is the everyday plural of person. Persons is not wrong, but it is confined to law, police reports, and signs — maximum occupancy 40 persons. Separately, people has its own singular sense meaning 'a nation', and that one pluralizes regularly: the peoples of the Pacific.

entries.meaning: A small numbered cube used in games; also, in manufacturing, a shaped tool for cutting or stamping.
examples: Roll the dice and move that many spaces.
He rolled a six on a single die.
Both dice came up threes.
The shop cut new dies for the replacement parts.
A hardened steel die stamps the pattern.
The die is cast — there's no going back now.
It was a roll of the dice, and it paid off.

senses.head: A gaming cube
body: Strictly the singular is die, but most American speakers say a dice, and die now sounds bookish outside board-game instructions. (игральная кость)
examples: Roll the dice and move that many spaces.
He rolled a six on a single die.
Both dice came up threes.

senses.head: A shaping or cutting tool
examples: The shop cut new dies for the replacement parts.
A hardened steel die stamps the pattern.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: The die is cast — there's no going back now.
It was a roll of the dice, and it paid off.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the dice are loaded
entries.pattern: suppletive in the gaming sense, regular in the tool sense
entries.variants: in casual American English dice is now often used for the singular too — roll a dice
entries.contrast: Two different plurals for two different senses. Gaming cubes: dice. Metal-shaping tools: dies. And be careful with the unrelated verb die 'to stop living', whose forms are dies, died, dying.

entries.meaning: The one-cent coin in the United States, or the British unit worth one hundredth of a pound.
examples: There were forty pennies at the bottom of the jar.
He paid the last dollar in pennies, which the cashier did not enjoy.
I found a penny on the sidewalk.
The stamp cost sixty pence.
A penny saved is a penny earned.
It didn't cost me a penny.
Then the penny dropped and I understood what she meant.
He pinches pennies but drives a new car.

senses.head: The coin as an object
examples: There were forty pennies at the bottom of the jar.
He paid the last dollar in pennies, which the cashier did not enjoy.
I found a penny on the sidewalk.

senses.head: An amount of British money
examples: The stamp cost sixty pence.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
body: Very frequent in American speech. (в устойчивых выражениях)
examples: A penny saved is a penny earned.
It didn't cost me a penny.
Then the penny dropped and I understood what she meant.
He pinches pennies but drives a new car.

entries.plural: pennies /ˈpɛniz/ (coins) · pence /pɛns/ (a British sum of money)
entries.agreement: plural verb — the pennies were in a jar
entries.pattern: regular -ies for objects, suppletive pence for amounts
entries.variants: American English uses pennies almost exclusively; pence belongs to British money
entries.contrast: The split is objects versus amounts. Count the coins and you have pennies; state a price and British English uses pence. In the United States the coin is a penny but the unit is a cent, so pence is rare in American speech outside quoting a British price.
